name: The Will to Believe
plain_explanation: James argues that in matters (especially religious ones) where the evidence is not conclusive either way, but where a decision cannot be avoided even by doing nothing, we have a right to choose to believe -- because avoiding error is not more important than believing truth, and refusing to decide risks missing out on truths a bolder person would have believed.
precise_definition: Published in 1896, James's doctrine that the duty of veracity consists of two coequal precepts, 'believe truth' and 'shun error,' and that since the sceptic wrongly privileges only the second, a person facing a forced, momentous, and evidentially undecidable option (paradigmatically religious belief) is entitled to adopt a believing attitude even though 'our merely logical intellect may not have been coerced.'
why_it_mattered: It was, in Russell's account, a transitional doctrine leading naturally to pragmatism's redefinition of truth, and functioned as James's defence of the right to religious belief in an age of scientific scepticism.
historical_origin: The Will to Believe (1896); Russell compares its underlying attitude to that of Rousseau's Savoyard vicar.
examples: The stranger-on-the-train example: not knowing a stranger's name, positive veracity might seem to license believing he is called 'Ebenezer Wilkes Smith' rather than merely suspending judgement.
objections: Russell: James never once mentions probability, yet almost every real question admits of some assessment of relative probability, which collapses the 'equal right to believe' argument (illustrated with a Chinese observer choosing among Confucianism, Buddhism, and Christianity, which cannot all be true).

Russell: James wrongly treats belief and disbelief as the only alternatives, ignoring the intermediate, common and rational state of acting on a working hypothesis while remaining open to further evidence.

Russell's own precept of veracity: give any hypothesis worth considering exactly the degree of credence the evidence warrants, and seek further evidence when the question is important -- 'plain common sense,' and 'quite different' from James's procedure.
competing_positions: Russell's evidentialist account of veracity (proportion belief to evidence)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Develops, in Russell's account, into James's full pragmatist theory of truth published in 1907.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Chiefly a defence of the right to religious belief in the absence of conclusive theoretical grounds.
